etymology: The English rendering of the Areopagus (Greek Areios Pagos, “hill of Ares/Mars”), the council-hill of Athens where Paul preached to the philosophers (Acts 17).
biblical_def: Mars' Hill is the Authorized Version's name for the Areopagus, the council-hill of Athens, where the apostle Paul, his spirit stirred by a city wholly given to idolatry, preached the living God to the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers. Standing in the midst of Mars' hill, Paul took the Athenians' own altar “TO THE UNKNOWN GOD” as his text and declared the God they ignorantly worshipped: the God who made the world and all things, who dwelleth not in temples made with hands, who giveth life and breath to all, and who now commandeth all men everywhere to repent, having appointed a day in which He will judge the world by the Man whom He raised from the dead. When they heard of the resurrection, some mocked, some delayed, but certain believed, among them Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris. The dictionary marks Mars' Hill as the great pattern of apostolic engagement with pagan thought. Paul neither flattered the philosophers nor borrowed their authority; he quoted their poets only to turn their own words against their idolatry, and pressed home creation, providence, repentance, resurrection, and judgment. The dictionary holds it against two errors: the accommodation that would soften the gospel to please the cultured despisers, and the withdrawal that would refuse to reason with them at all. Paul did neither—he proclaimed the whole counsel of God to the wise of this world, and God called His own out of Athens by the foolishness of preaching.
webster_summary: The Areopagus at Athens where Paul preached the living God to the philosophers (Acts 17:22-34); the pattern of apostolic engagement with pagan thought—neither flattering nor withdrawing, but proclaiming creation, repentance, resurrection, and judgment.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the errors are the accommodation that softens the gospel to please cultured despisers, and the withdrawal that refuses to reason with the world at all.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is faithful apostolic engagement with the thought of the age. One corruption reads Paul at Athens as a model of accommodation—trimming the offensive parts, borrowing the philosophers' authority, blending the gospel with the culture's wisdom to win a hearing. But Paul did the opposite: he quoted a pagan poet only to turn the words against idolatry, and pressed home creation, repentance, resurrection, and a fixed day of judgment—the very points his hearers found most foolish. He won some not by softening the message but by proclaiming it.

The opposite corruption is withdrawal—the refusal to reason with the world at all, treating every engagement with pagan thought as compromise. Paul disputed daily in the market and reasoned on Mars' hill; he met the philosophers on their ground and answered them with the truth. The dictionary holds the balance the apostle struck: neither the accommodation that empties the cross of its offence, nor the retreat that hides the light under a bushel, but the bold, reasoned proclamation of the whole counsel of God to the wise of this world—trusting God to call His own out of Athens by the foolishness of preaching.

etymology: From the inscription Paul found at Athens, “TO THE UNKNOWN GOD” (Greek Agnosto Theo); the deity the Athenians worshipped in ignorance, whom Paul declared to be the true Creator.
biblical_def: The “unknown god” was the deity to whom the Athenians had raised an altar inscribed “TO THE UNKNOWN GOD,” hedging against any divinity they might have overlooked in their crowded pantheon. Paul seized upon it: “Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.” He proclaimed the God they did not know to be the one true God who made the world and all things, the Lord of heaven and earth who dwelleth not in temples made with hands, who gives to all life and breath and all things, and in whom we live and move and have our being. The dictionary marks the unknown god as a witness to two truths of natural revelation and its limits. First, fallen man has an inescapable awareness of God: the Athenians knew there was a divinity beyond their idols, and reached after Him, for the invisible things of God are clearly seen in the things that are made, so that they are without excuse. Second, this natural knowledge cannot save: it left the Athenians worshipping ignorantly, groping after a God they could not name, until the gospel declared Him. The dictionary holds the inscription against the modern pluralism that would treat all worship as worship of the same God under different names—as though the Athenian idols and the living God were one. Paul allowed no such thing: he called their devotion ignorance and their idols vanity, and declared the unknown God to be the Creator and Judge who now commands all men everywhere to repent. The God whom nature reveals as real, only Christ reveals as Saviour.
webster_summary: The deity of the Athenian altar “TO THE UNKNOWN GOD” (Acts 17:23), whom Paul declared the true Creator; a witness that fallen man knows God exists (Romans 1:20) yet cannot name or be saved by Him apart from the gospel.

corruption_summary: Modern pluralism reads the unknown god as proof that all religions worship the same God under different names; Paul allowed no such thing, calling the Athenian devotion ignorance and declaring the one true Creator.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the truth and the limit of natural revelation. The pluralism of the age seizes on the unknown god to argue that all worship is worship of the same God under different names—that the Athenian idols and the living God are one, and that Paul merely “named what they already knew.” Paul allowed no such thing. He called their worship ignorant and their devotions idolatry, and declared the unknown God to be the one Creator and Judge, not a member of their pantheon. The gospel does not affirm the nations' gods; it calls men to turn from them to the living God.

Yet the inscription also witnesses to the real, if insufficient, knowledge fallen man retains. The Athenians knew there was a divinity beyond their idols and reached after Him, for the invisible things of God are clearly seen in creation, leaving every man without excuse. The dictionary holds both truths against the pluralist and the atheist alike: man knows God exists, for nature declares Him; but man cannot name or be saved by that God apart from the special revelation of the gospel. The unknown God of the altar is the known God of the cross—and Him Paul declared.

etymology: From Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus council, converted under Paul's preaching at Athens (Acts 17:34); later the falsely-attributed author of the “Pseudo-Dionysian” mystical writings.
biblical_def: Dionysius the Areopagite was a member of the Athenian council of the Areopagus who, when most mocked or delayed at Paul's preaching of the resurrection, clave unto the apostle and believed. He stands in Acts as living proof that the gospel reached even the cultured and powerful of Athens—a counsellor of the city among the firstfruits of Greece, alongside the woman Damaris and others. Though not many wise men after the flesh are called, God called this one, that no class of men might think itself beyond the reach of grace. The dictionary honours the historical Dionysius as a true convert and a token of the gospel's power among the learned. It must, however, sharply distinguish him from the body of mystical writings later forged in his name. In the late fifth or early sixth century an unknown author, steeped in Neoplatonism, composed treatises on the divine names, the celestial and ecclesiastical hierarchies, and mystical theology, and passed them off under the prestige of the apostolic convert. These “Pseudo-Dionysian” writings exercised vast and harmful influence on medieval mysticism, hierarchy, and the doctrine of God, importing a Neoplatonic ladder of being and an apophatic mysticism foreign to Scripture. The dictionary names the forgery for what it is and applies the apostolic rule: prove all things, hold fast that which is good. The true Dionysius is honoured as an Athenian trophy of grace; the writings stolen for his name are weighed by the Word and found wanting, a warning that a venerable name is no guarantee of sound doctrine.
webster_summary: The Athenian Areopagite converted under Paul's preaching (Acts 17:34), a trophy of grace among the learned; sharply distinguished from the later Neoplatonic “Pseudo-Dionysian” writings forged in his name, which the dictionary names a forgery to be weighed by the Word.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary honours the historical Dionysius as a genuine convert and a token of the gospel's power among the learned and powerful of Athens. Though not many wise after the flesh are called, God called this counsellor of the Areopagus, that no class of men might count itself beyond the reach of grace. The corruption attaches not to the man but to the forgery done in his name. In the late fifth or early sixth century an anonymous author steeped in Neoplatonism wrote treatises—on the divine names, the celestial and ecclesiastical hierarchies, and mystical theology—and passed them off under the prestige of the apostolic convert. etymology: A traditional name for the three graces of 1 Corinthians 13:13 — faith, hope, and charity (love); “theological” because they have God for their object and are wrought by His grace.
biblical_def: The theological virtues are faith, hope, and charity (love)—the three abiding graces the apostle names together: “And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.” They are called theological because they have God Himself for their object and source: faith lays hold of God's truth and His Christ; hope rests on God's promise of glory; love embraces God and, for His sake, the neighbour. They are not natural attainments but graces wrought by the Spirit, distinguished in the older theology from the “cardinal” or natural virtues (prudence, justice, temperance, fortitude). Paul joins the three repeatedly: the Thessalonians' work of faith, labour of love, and patience of hope; the believer's breastplate of faith and love and helmet of the hope of salvation. The dictionary receives the triad as a true and useful summary of the Christian graces, while correcting the Roman framework in which it has often been set. Rome treats the theological virtues as infused habits that, cooperating with works, contribute to a justification by inherent righteousness. The dictionary holds rather that faith is the instrument by which the sinner is justified—receiving Christ's imputed righteousness, not its own—and that hope and love are the fruits and companions of that justifying faith, not co-causes of acceptance with God. So understood, the three abide: faith and hope have their use in this life of pilgrimage and pass into sight and possession in glory, but love abides for ever and is the greatest, for God is love, and the redeemed shall love Him perfectly when faith is sight and hope is fulfilled.
webster_summary: Faith, hope, and charity—the three abiding graces (1 Corinthians 13:13), called “theological” because they have God for their object and source; received as a true summary, with faith as the justifying instrument and love the greatest, against the Roman infused-merit framework.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary receives the triad of faith, hope, and charity as a true and useful summary of the Christian graces, which have God for their object and are wrought by His Spirit. The correction needed is doctrinal, against the Roman framework in which the triad has often been set. Rome treats the theological virtues as infused habits that, cooperating with the believer's works, contribute to a justification grounded in inherent righteousness—so that “faith formed by love” justifies by what it does. This confounds justification with sanctification and overthrows the gospel of grace.

The dictionary holds the Reformation distinction. Faith justifies not as a virtue that merits, but as the empty hand that receives Christ's imputed righteousness; the sinner is accepted for Christ's righteousness, not his own faith, hope, or love. Hope and love are the inseparable fruits and companions of justifying faith—real, necessary, and abiding—but not co-causes of acceptance with God. So the three abide: faith passes into sight and hope into possession when the pilgrim reaches glory, but love abides for ever and is the greatest, for God is love, and the redeemed shall love Him perfectly when faith is sight and hope fulfilled.

pos: noun phrase (a method of defending the faith)
etymology: From “presupposition” (a foundational assumption) and “apologetics”; the Reformed method, associated with Cornelius Van Til, that defends the faith by exposing the unbeliever's borrowed assumptions and the self-attesting authority of Scripture.
biblical_def: Presuppositional apologetics is the method of defending the Christian faith, developed chiefly by Cornelius Van Til and his successors, that begins not from supposedly neutral ground but from the self-attesting authority of God's revelation, and exposes the borrowed and self-defeating assumptions of unbelief. Its convictions are thoroughly Reformed. There is no neutral ground: every man reasons from ultimate commitments, and the unbeliever, though he knows God, suppresses the truth in unrighteousness, so that his very arguments against God secretly borrow from the Christian worldview the intelligibility, logic, and morality that only God supplies. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, and in Christ are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; therefore the apologist does not lend the autonomous reason of fallen man the authority to judge God, but casts down imaginations and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ. God hath made foolish the wisdom of this world. The dictionary commends presuppositional apologetics as the method most consistent with total depravity and the authority of Scripture, against the “classical” or “evidentialist” methods that grant fallen reason a neutral seat of judgment and try to build up to God from autonomous premises. It marks two cautions: that the method must still press the abundant evidence and reason with men, not merely assert; and that its aim is not to win an argument but to expose the folly of unbelief and call the sinner to repentance, for no apologetic converts—only the Spirit gives the heart of flesh that bows to the truth.
webster_summary: The Reformed apologetic method (Cornelius Van Til) that defends the faith from the self-attesting authority of Scripture and exposes unbelief's borrowed, self-defeating assumptions (2 Corinthians 10:5); consistent with total depravity, against neutral-ground evidentialism.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter is a difference of method among believers, in which the dictionary takes a considered side. The classical and evidentialist methods grant fallen reason a neutral seat of judgment, building up to God from premises the unbeliever is asked to weigh as an impartial judge. The dictionary regards this as inconsistent with total depravity and the authority of Scripture: there is no neutral ground, for the natural man suppresses the truth, and to let him judge God by autonomous reason is to concede the very point in dispute. Presuppositional apologetics begins rightly—from the self-attesting God—and exposes that the unbeliever must borrow from the Christian worldview the logic and morality he uses to deny it.

The dictionary commends the method while marking two cautions, lest it be abused. First, presuppositionalism is not an excuse for mere assertion or for refusing to reason; Paul disputed daily and pressed the resurrection's evidence, and the apologist must still answer fools according to their folly and set forth the abundant proofs God has given. Second, no method converts. The aim is not to win a debate but to expose the folly of unbelief and call the sinner to repentance; the bowing of the proud mind to Christ is the work of the Spirit, who gives the heart of flesh. The best apologetic, faithfully pressed, only removes excuses—God alone removes the stony heart.

etymology: Greek Pantainos; a converted Stoic philosopher of the second century, head of the catechetical school of Alexandria and teacher of Clement of Alexandria.
biblical_def: Pantaenus was a Christian teacher of the late second century, a converted Stoic philosopher who became head of the catechetical school of Alexandria and the teacher of Clement of Alexandria. Tradition reports that he labored as a missionary as far as “India” (perhaps southern Arabia or the Indian subcontinent), and that he found there believers already acquainted with the Gospel of Matthew. As a teacher he committed the things he had learned to faithful men able to teach others, after the apostolic charge, and helped make Alexandria a centre of Christian learning. The dictionary honours Pantaenus as an early example of the consecration of learning to Christ and of the missionary impulse that carried the gospel far beyond the Roman world—a man who, like Paul before the philosophers, brought a trained mind into captivity to the obedience of Christ and taught others to do the same. Yet the dictionary marks the school he led with the caution proper to Alexandria. The catechetical school, under Pantaenus and especially his successors Clement and Origen, married Christian teaching to Greek philosophy and pioneered the allegorical method of interpreting Scripture that the dictionary elsewhere names a corruption—reading hidden meanings into the text and subordinating the plain sense to philosophical speculation. The dictionary applies its rule for figures outside the Reformed tradition: honour the genuine zeal, learning, and missionary labour of Pantaenus, while naming the allegorizing and the over-marriage of faith and philosophy that grew in the school he helped found. A trained mind devoted to Christ is a gift; a method that bends Scripture to philosophy is a danger, and both met in Alexandria.
webster_summary: A converted Stoic and head of the catechetical school of Alexandria (late 2nd c.), teacher of Clement and reputed missionary to “India”; honoured for learning and zeal devoted to Christ, with the school's allegorizing and over-marriage of faith and philosophy named.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary honours the genuine good in Pantaenus: a trained Stoic mind converted and consecrated to Christ, a teacher who committed the faith to faithful men able to teach others, and a missionary reputed to have carried the gospel far beyond the Roman world. The consecration of learning to Christ and the missionary impulse are honourable, and Alexandria under his hand became a centre where the faith engaged the best thought of the age.

Yet the dictionary marks the danger that grew in the school he founded. Under Pantaenus and especially his successors Clement and Origen, the catechetical school married Christian teaching to Greek philosophy and pioneered the allegorical interpretation of Scripture—reading hidden meanings into the text and subordinating its plain sense to philosophical speculation, the method the dictionary names a corruption. Applying its rule for figures outside the Reformed tradition, the dictionary honours the man's zeal, learning, and labour while naming the allegorizing and the over-marriage of faith and philosophy as the school's lasting harm. A mind devoted to Christ is a gift; a method that bends the Word to philosophy is a peril, and both met at Alexandria.

etymology: From “catechetical” (of instruction, Greek katecheo); chiefly the catechetical school of Alexandria, the early centre of Christian learning under Pantaenus, Clement, and Origen.
biblical_def: The catechetical school most famously names the school of Alexandria, the early and influential centre of Christian instruction and scholarship that flourished from the late second century under Pantaenus, Clement of Alexandria, and Origen. Founded to instruct converts and catechumens in the faith, it grew into a centre of advanced theological learning where Christianity engaged the philosophy, science, and literature of the Hellenistic world. The dictionary weighs the school with discrimination. Its commendable aim was real: the careful instruction of believers in the faith and the training of teachers, in the spirit of the apostolic charge to instruct, that men might know the certainty of the things wherein they were catechized, and to train up the young in the way they should go. The defence of the faith before a learned pagan world was a worthy labour. But the dictionary names the school's besetting fault: it pioneered and propagated the allegorical method of interpreting Scripture, treating the literal sense as a husk to be discarded for hidden spiritual meanings, and it married Christian doctrine too closely to Neoplatonic philosophy—errors that reached their height in Origen, whose speculations (on the pre-existence of souls, universal restoration, and the subordination of the Son) departed gravely from the faith. Against the school of Alexandria stood the school of Antioch, with its sounder literal-historical method, which the Reformers' own exegesis followed. The dictionary honours the catechetical school's zeal for learning and instruction while naming its allegorizing and philosophical entanglement as the seedbed of much later error, holding that the church's schools must instruct the young in sound doctrine and the plain sense of the Word, no prophecy of Scripture being of any private interpretation.
webster_summary: The early centre of Christian learning at Alexandria (Pantaenus, Clement, Origen); honoured for its zeal to instruct and engage the learned world, yet named the seedbed of allegorical exegesis and Neoplatonic entanglement, against the sounder school of Antioch.
webster_full: CATECHETICAL SCHOOL, noun phrase. [Greek katecheo, to instruct.] Chiefly the school of Alexandria.
Flourished from the late 2nd century under Pantaenus, Clement, and Origen.
Founded to instruct converts; grew into a centre of theological learning.
Pioneered the allegorical method and married doctrine to Neoplatonic philosophy.
Opposed by the sounder literal-historical school of Antioch.
scriptures: Lu 1:4
That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed.
This man was instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in the spirit, he spake and taught diligently the things of the Lord, knowing only the baptism of John.
Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
corruption_summary: The school of Alexandria pioneered allegorical exegesis and married doctrine to Neoplatonic philosophy, errors that reached their height in Origen's grave speculations.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary honours the catechetical school's commendable aim—the careful instruction of converts in the faith and the training of teachers, that men might know the certainty of the things wherein they were catechized. To instruct the young in sound doctrine and to defend the faith before a learned pagan world is honourable labour, and Alexandria gathered real gifts to that end.

Yet the dictionary names the school's besetting faults. It pioneered and propagated the allegorical method of interpreting Scripture, discarding the literal sense for hidden meanings, and it married Christian doctrine too closely to Neoplatonic philosophy. These errors reached their height in Origen, whose speculations on the pre-existence of souls, universal restoration, and the subordination of the Son departed gravely from the faith. Against Alexandria stood the school of Antioch, with its sounder literal-historical exegesis, which the Reformers' own interpretation followed. The dictionary holds that the church's schools must instruct in sound doctrine and the plain sense of the Word, remembering that no prophecy of Scripture is of any private interpretation—honouring the zeal of Alexandria while refusing the method that became the seedbed of much later error.
roots_summary: From the Greek katecheo (to instruct by word of mouth), whence “catechetical”; the Alexandrian school of instruction that became a centre of theological learning.
roots_lines: Katecheo, Greek, to instruct, the root of “catechetical.”
The school of Alexandria, founded to instruct converts and catechumens.
Led successively by Pantaenus, Clement of Alexandria, and Origen.
Pioneer of the allegorical method of interpreting Scripture.
Opposed by the literal-historical school of Antioch.
usage: The teacher honoured the catechetical school's zeal to instruct while naming its allegorizing.
He traced Origen's grave speculations to the school's marriage of doctrine and philosophy.
She held that the church's schools must teach the plain sense of the Word, not private interpretation.

etymology: The Epistle of Clement of Rome to the Corinthians (c. A.D. 96), the earliest surviving Christian writing outside the New Testament; reckoned among the Apostolic Fathers.
biblical_def: First Clement is the letter written about A.D. 96 from the church at Rome, in the name of Clement, to the church at Corinth, the earliest surviving Christian writing outside the New Testament canon and a chief witness among the Apostolic Fathers. Its occasion was a renewed outbreak of the Corinthian disease the apostle Paul had rebuked decades earlier: a faction in the church had risen up and deposed its godly elders, and the Roman church wrote to call them back to order, humility, and submission. The letter is saturated with Scripture, exalts the gospel of justification, urges humility—for God resisteth the proud and giveth grace to the humble—and pleads for peace and the restoration of the lawfully-appointed elders. The dictionary values First Clement as an early and edifying witness: it shows the next generation after the apostles holding the same Scriptures, the same gospel, and the same concern for godly church order, and it earnestly contended for the faith once delivered. Yet the dictionary holds it firmly in its place, against two errors. The first would press First Clement toward the canon, as some early churches nearly did; but it is not inspired Scripture, however valuable, and the canon is closed at the sixty-six books. The second, graver error reads into First Clement—a letter from the Roman church urging order—a proof of early Roman primacy and papal authority, as Rome has done. The dictionary denies the inference: a sister church's fraternal exhortation to another is not the rule of a bishop over the universal church, and First Clement nowhere claims for Rome the supremacy later ages invented. It is an Apostolic Father's letter, honoured as a faithful early witness, weighed by the Word, and granted no authority above it.
webster_summary: The letter from the church at Rome to Corinth (c. A.D. 96), earliest Christian writing outside the canon, urging the restoration of deposed elders; an edifying Apostolic-Father witness—not inspired Scripture, and no proof of Roman primacy.
webster_full: 1 CLEMENT, proper noun. The epistle of Clement of Rome to the Corinthians, c. A.D. 96.
The earliest surviving Christian writing outside the New Testament.
It rebuked a Corinthian faction that had deposed its godly elders.
Saturated with Scripture, exalting the gospel and urging humility (1 Peter 5:5).
An edifying Apostolic-Father witness—not inspired Scripture, and no proof of Roman primacy.
scriptures: Php 4:3
And I intreat thee also, true yokefellow, help those women which laboured with me in the gospel, with Clement also, and with other my fellowlabourers, whose names are in the book of life.

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility: for God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.
corruption_summary: One error presses 1 Clement toward the canon; the graver error reads into it a proof of early Roman primacy and papal authority, which the letter nowhere claims.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary values First Clement as an early and edifying witness—the generation after the apostles holding the same Scriptures, the same gospel of justification, and the same concern for godly church order, earnestly contending for the faith once delivered and pleading for humility and peace at Corinth. As a window into the post-apostolic church, it is precious. But it must be held in its place. The first error would press it toward the canon, as some early churches nearly did; the dictionary holds it not inspired Scripture, however valuable, the canon being closed at the sixty-six books.

The graver error is Rome's. Because the letter comes from the church at Rome and urges the Corinthians to restore order, Rome reads into it a proof of early Roman primacy—the bishop of Rome already ruling the universal church. The dictionary denies the inference plainly. A sister church's fraternal exhortation to another, however weighty, is not the rule of a bishop over all; First Clement is written in the name of the church at Rome, not a monarchical pope, and it nowhere claims the supremacy later ages invented. It is an Apostolic Father's letter—honoured as a faithful early witness, weighed by the Word, and granted no authority above it, and certainly no warrant for the papal claims built upon it.
roots_summary: Attributed to Clement of Rome, possibly the Clement of Philippians 4:3; the first of the writings of the Apostolic Fathers, written from the Roman church to Corinth.
roots_lines: Clement of Rome, the traditional author, possibly the Clement of Philippians 4:3.
Written c. A.D. 96 from the church at Rome to the church at Corinth.
The earliest surviving Christian writing outside the New Testament.
Reckoned among the Apostolic Fathers.
Occasioned by a Corinthian faction's deposing of its elders.
usage: The teacher valued 1 Clement as an early witness to the same gospel and church order as the apostles.
He held it edifying but not inspired Scripture, the canon being closed.
She denied that a Roman church's fraternal letter proved the papal primacy Rome later claimed.

etymology: From the Authorized Version rendering of the Greek ethelothreskeia (Colossians 2:23), “self-imposed worship”; worship devised by the will of man rather than commanded by God.
biblical_def: Will worship is worship devised by the will of man rather than commanded by God—the Authorized Version's rendering of the Greek ethelothreskeia, “self-chosen religion.” The apostle warns the Colossians against the ordinances and traditions of men, which “have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.” Such worship looks pious—ascetic, humble, severe—but it is self-invented, resting on the commandments and doctrines of men, and the Lord pronounces it vain: “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.” The dictionary marks will worship as the precise opposite of the regulative principle of worship, which holds that God is to be worshipped only in the ways He has appointed in His Word. Whatsoever God commands in worship is required; whatsoever He has not commanded is forbidden, for He charged Israel, “What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.” Will worship is the sin of adding—the will of man legislating for God how He shall be served. The dictionary marks it against the whole tide of self-styled worship: the inventions of Rome (images, relics, the multiplied rites and feasts), the asceticism that supposes self-denial earns merit, and equally the modern self-expressive worship that makes the worshipper's preference and feeling the rule, asking not “what has God commanded?” but “what do we like?” Both the old severity and the new spontaneity are will worship if they rest on the will of man rather than the Word of God. True worship is humble obedience: God to be served as He has prescribed, neither more nor less.
webster_summary: Worship devised by the will of man rather than commanded by God (Colossians 2:23, Greek ethelothreskeia); the opposite of the regulative principle, condemned as vain (Matthew 15:9) whether in ascetic invention or modern self-expression.
webster_full: WILL WORSHIP, noun phrase. [Greek ethelothreskeia, self-chosen religion.] Worship devised by man's will, not God's command.
It has “a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility… not in any honour” (Colossians 2:23).
The Lord calls it vain: teaching for doctrines the commandments of men (Matthew 15:9).
The opposite of the regulative principle: God adds nor diminishes (Deuteronomy 12:32).
Found alike in ascetic invention and in modern self-expressive worship.
scriptures: Col 2:23
Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.
corruption_summary: Will worship is itself the corruption: man's will legislating for God how He shall be served—found in Rome's ascetic inventions and equally in modern self-expressive worship that asks “what do we like?” not “what has God commanded?”
corruption_paragraphs: Will worship is the corruption to be named, not a doctrine at risk of drift. It is worship invented by the will of man and not commanded by God, and the apostle exposes it: it has a show of wisdom—ascetic, humble, severe—but rests on the commandments and doctrines of men, and the Lord calls such worship vain. The dictionary sets against it the regulative principle: God is to be worshipped only as He has appointed, for He forbids adding to or diminishing from what He commands. To devise worship He has not authorized, however pious it appears, is to put the will of man in the place of the Word of God.

The dictionary marks two faces of the same sin. The old face is the ascetic and ceremonial invention—Rome's images, relics, multiplied rites and feasts, and the self-denial that supposes it earns merit. The new face, equally will worship, is the modern self-expressive worship that makes the worshipper's preference and feeling the rule, asking not “what has God commanded?” but “what moves us?” The dictionary names both: whether the will of man invents severity or invents spontaneity, it is still the will of man legislating for God. True worship is humble obedience—God served in the ways He has prescribed, neither more nor less, that the honour be His and not the worshipper's.
roots_summary: From the Greek ethelothreskeia (Colossians 2:23), from thelo (to will) and threskeia (religion, worship); “self-willed worship,” rendered “will worship” in the Authorized Version.
roots_lines: Ethelothreskeia, Greek, “self-chosen worship” (Colossians 2:23).
Thelo, Greek, to will or wish; threskeia, religion or worship.
The opposite of the regulative principle of worship.
Condemned as vain: “the commandments of men” (Matthew 15:9).
Forbidden by the rule against adding to God's commands (Deuteronomy 12:32).
usage: The pastor named the unbiblical rite will worship, a show of wisdom resting on the will of man.
He applied the regulative principle: God adds nor diminishes, and will worship is the sin of adding.
She saw that both ascetic invention and self-expressive worship are will worship if they rest on man's will.

etymology: From the Latin bene (well) and velle (to wish); the goodness of God considered as His good-will toward His creatures, doing them good.
biblical_def: The benevolence of God is the goodness of God considered as His good-will toward His creatures—His disposition to do them good and the kindness by which He actually does it. It is an aspect of the divine goodness, that perfection by which God is in Himself infinitely good and is the fountain of all good to His works. “The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works,” says the Psalmist; “the LORD is good; his mercy is everlasting.” This benevolence appears in two ranges. There is a general benevolence—often called common grace—by which God does good to all without distinction: He maketh His sun to rise on the evil and on the good, sendeth rain on the just and the unjust, fills men's hearts with food and gladness, and gives every good and perfect gift from above, with whom is no variableness. And there is His special, saving benevolence toward His elect, the everlasting love by which He chose, redeemed, and will glorify His people. The dictionary marks the benevolence of God against two errors. The first, a sentimental universalism, so magnifies God's general goodness as to deny His justice, holiness, and wrath—making benevolence the only attribute and concluding that He will save all and punish none. But the same God who is good to all is also just, and His benevolence does not cancel His holiness. The second error so fears that sentimentality that it underplays God's genuine kindness even to the wicked and His tender mercy to His own. The dictionary holds the balance Scripture holds: God is truly and abundantly good, the giver of every good gift, tender in mercy over all His works—and that goodness is never severed from His justice, but crowned, for the elect, in the unspeakable gift of His Son.
webster_summary: The goodness of God as His good-will toward His creatures (Psalm 145:9; Psalm 100:5); seen in general benevolence (common grace) to all and special saving love to the elect—abundant yet never severed from His justice and holiness.
webster_full: BENEVOLENCE OF GOD, noun phrase. [Latin bene velle, to wish well.] God's good-will toward His creatures, doing them good.
“The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works” (Psalm 145:9).
General benevolence (common grace): sun and rain on just and unjust (Matthew 5:45).
Special saving benevolence: His everlasting love toward the elect.
Abundant goodness, never severed from His justice and holiness.
scriptures: The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.
That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.
For the LORD is good; his mercy is everlasting; and his truth endureth to all generations.
Jas 1:17
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
corruption_summary: Sentimental universalism magnifies God's benevolence until it cancels His justice and wrath; the opposite error underplays His genuine kindness to the wicked and tender mercy to His own.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the goodness of God held together with His justice. The first corruption is a sentimental universalism that so magnifies the divine benevolence as to make it the only attribute—concluding that a good God will save all and punish none, that love cancels wrath, and that holiness must yield to kindness. The dictionary answers that the same God who is good to all is also just, holy, and a consuming fire; His benevolence is real and abundant but never severed from His other perfections, for in the simplicity of God all His attributes are one. A goodness that excludes justice is not the goodness of the God of Scripture.

The opposite error, in dread of sentimentality, so stresses God's wrath and justice that it underplays His genuine kindness—forgetting that He is good to all, sends rain on the unjust, fills men with food and gladness, and is tender in mercy over all His works, and that toward His own His benevolence rises to the unspeakable gift of His Son. The dictionary holds the balance Scripture holds: God is truly, abundantly, and tenderly good, the fountain and giver of every good and perfect gift; and that goodness, far from cancelling His justice, is crowned for the elect in the cross, where benevolence and justice meet and kiss.
roots_summary: From the Latin bene (well) and velle (to wish); an aspect of the divine goodness (Hebrew tov; Greek agathosune), God's good-will toward His creatures.
roots_lines: Bene velle, Latin, “to wish well,” the root of “benevolence.”
Tov, Hebrew, good; “the LORD is good to all” (Psalm 145:9).
Agathosune, Greek, goodness, a fruit of the Spirit and a perfection of God.
General benevolence (common grace) toward all; special benevolence toward the elect.
Held together with God's justice and holiness in the simplicity of His being.
usage: The teacher preached the benevolence of God, good to all, yet never severed from His justice.
He answered the universalist that a goodness which cancels wrath is not the God of Scripture.
She gave thanks for every good gift from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness.
